title: Trump again floats Ted Cruz for Supreme Court if a seat opens - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
Trump told a Lubbock crowd he’d pick Ted Cruz for the next Supreme Court vacancy, predicting unanimous confirmation because both parties want him gone.
President Trump told a midterm rally in Lubbock, Texas, that Sen. Ted Cruz would be his choice for the next opening on the Supreme Court, framing the idea as a sure thing in the Senate.
The Hill reported the Tuesday remarks, in which Trump cast the Texas Republican as a brilliant lawyer with top credentials and joked that Democrats and Republicans alike would rush to confirm him just to remove him from Congress.
No vacancy was announced. The pitch was hypothetical. Still, it fits a pattern: Trump has floated Cruz for the high court more than once, and Cruz has already made clear he wants to stay in the political fight.
Trump opened by pointing to his own record. He named the three justices he put on the Court in his first term, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, and said confirmations remain a grind.
“I picked three Supreme Court justices, and it’s very hard to get them approved.”
Then he offered what he called an answer.
“I said, ‘Look, I have an answer to it.’ Ted is a brilliant guy, brilliant lawyer, brilliant all that.”
He kept going on credentials and politics in the same breath.
“Went to law school, top student, everything, top credentials. I said, ‘I have an answer to not being able to get it past the Democrats or the Republicans together.’ I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice.”
Both parties, he said, would vote yes to clear Cruz out
Trump’s punch line was institutional, not personal praise alone. He predicted Democrats would back the nomination “100 percent” because, in his words, “they hate the guy and they want to get rid of him.”
He said Republicans would do the same.
“And the Republicans would 100 percent vote for it because they can’t stand him. They would like to get rid of him. So I’d get 100 percent of the vote, and he would be a Supreme Court justice, and he’d do a great job.”
The joke lands because Cruz has long been a polarizing figure inside Washington, not only across the aisle. Trump treated that friction as a confirmation strategy: nominate the senator both sides would rather see leave the Capitol.
Readers tracking court fights and pushback against Trump will recognize the broader climate, including cases where an federal judge extends freeze on administration action and other legal skirmishes that keep the judiciary in the headlines.
Cruz already said no, three times
Cruz has not treated the idea as a dream job. He has said he does not plan to trade his Senate seat for a lifetime appointment.
At an April event hosted by The Wall Street Journal, described as an “Opinion Live” interview, Cruz said Trump has spoken to him “seriously” about filling a hypothetical vacancy. He also explained why he walked away before.
“In the first Trump term, the president spoke to me seriously about all three vacancies, and three times I said no, because I don’t want to be out of the arena of the political battle.”
That stance is consistent. Cruz frames his work as policy combat in the elected branch, not only legal argument from the bench. A seat on the Supreme Court is powerful. It is also removed from the day-to-day fights he says he still wants.
Trump’s Lubbock line was not the first time he has run the bit. Earlier this year, during a July White House event promoting Trump Accounts, he made a similar joke about putting Cruz on the Court.
The repetition matters. Trump is not floating a random name. He is circling a senator he calls brilliant, with a law-school record and courtroom credentials, while Cruz keeps choosing the Senate floor over the marble.
Separate fights over the courts continue elsewhere, including when Jim Jordan seeks misconduct probe of an Obama-appointed judge tied to sanctions on a Trump lawyer, another reminder that judicial power and political conflict stay tightly linked.
Credentials first, Capitol math second
Strip away the laugh line and Trump’s public case still rests on two claims the Lubbock crowd heard plainly. First, Cruz has the résumé. Second, the confirmation math would be easy for the wrong reasons, because colleagues want him gone.
Whether that second claim is sharp politics or pure showmanship, Trump stated it without hedging. He did not describe a quiet shortlist. He described a nominee both parties would rubber-stamp to empty a Senate desk.
Cruz’s reply, already on the record from the spring, undercuts any rush narrative. He said no three times when it was serious. He said he wants to remain in the arena. Nothing in the latest rally remarks shows him reversing that.
Trump’s midterm swing through Texas put the line back in front of voters anyway. Lubbock heard the praise, the Court résumé, and the unanimous-vote gag in one package. The Hill’s account ties those remarks to the same theme Trump used at the White House in July.
Campaign seasons produce a lot of stage talk. This one connects to real history: three prior Trump justices, prior private conversations Cruz himself described, and a senator who keeps choosing elections and legislation over a robe.
Other Trump-cycle stories keep the same audience moving, from Trump offers $1 million for tips aimed at convicting voter fraudsters to sharper media clashes after public events.
For now there is no open seat and no nomination to score. There is a president revisiting a familiar name, a résumé he likes, and a confirmation theory built on Cruz’s talent for making enemies in both parties.
Cruz’s own words still point the other way. He wants the political battle, not a quieter chamber across the street. Trump can keep joking. The senator has already answered the serious version.
Recent coverage of Trump’s public schedule has also included lighter political scrapes, such as when Trump’s brief Air Force One stair slip set off another round of critic attacks, noise that rarely slows the larger personnel and court conversation.
Washington will keep arguing over judges, nominees, and who belongs on the nation’s highest court. Voters can tell the difference between a rally laugh line and a papered nomination.
When Trump praises a fighter’s credentials and that fighter still chooses the arena, conservatives get a clear signal about who wants the robe, and who still wants the fight.
